question: How do maximum likelihood, the bootstrap and Bayesian inference relate, and how can bootstrap, model averaging, stacking and bumping improve a fitted model?
contributions: Shows least squares, parametric bootstrap and maximum likelihood agree for Gaussian-error models
Relates bootstrap to noninformative Bayes posterior
Presents EM (and Gibbs sampling as its stochastic analogue)
Presents bagging, Bayesian model averaging, stacking and bumping

limits: Bootstrap-posterior correspondence holds exactly only for Gaussian models; multinomial case is approximate (Sec 8.4).
EM finds a local maximum; the global likelihood maximum of a Gaussian mixture is degenerate (infinite spike), so initialisation matters (p274).
Bagging argument works for squared error; fails for 0-1 loss and bagging a bad classifier can make it worse (p285-286).
Bagging loses interpretability (a bagged tree is no longer a tree) and does not help stable procedures like nearest neighbours (p286).
Authors say they have seen no real evidence full Bayesian model averaging is worth the effort versus the BIC approximation (p289).
Bumping needs models of roughly equal complexity (p292).
All examples are small simulated or fictitious data (N=20 to 100); no real benchmark.
practices: Use the bootstrap to get standard errors and bands when no formula exists, e.g. when knots are chosen adaptively by cross-validation (Sec 8.2.3, p267).
Resample (x,y) pairs for the nonparametric bootstrap; use B=200 as the worked choice (p264).
Initialise EM mu estimates from two random observations, sigma^2 at the overall sample variance, pi at 0.5; run several starts and keep the highest likelihood with sigma_k^2 > 0.5 (p274).
When bagging classifiers, average class-probability estimates rather than vote indicators for better probabilities and lower variance, especially at small B (p283).
Bag unstable, adaptive procedures such as trees; bagging a linear smoother returns the original fit (p282).
Use stacking with leave-one-out predictions to weight models so complexity is not rewarded; restricting weights to be nonnegative and sum to 1 gives a tractable quadratic program (p290).
Use BIC as a simple approximation to posterior model probabilities for averaging (p289).
In Gibbs sampling, average the conditional density over iterations M-m+1 after a burn-in (Eq 8.50, p280).
Proper (non-improper) priors are needed on mixture means in Gibbs sampling, otherwise the posterior degenerates (p282).
For bumping, grow trees with the same number of terminal nodes on each bootstrap sample and include the original sample among the candidates (p291-292).
